summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct is lawful in Vietnam and has never been criminalised in Vietnamese history. The Penal Code sets the age of consent at 16 without regard to gender or sexual orientation. The 1812 Gia Long Code, Article 332, prohibited prostitution and illicit sexual activity including extra-marital sex, and prosecutions of homosexual conduct could in rare cases be brought under those labels, but enforcement before the colonial period was inconsistent and little to no state action is recorded.

Official hostility has a documented history. In 2002 the Ministry of Labour, Invalids and Social Affairs declared homosexuality a "social evil" comparable to prostitution, gambling and drug use, and promised legislation to combat homosexuality and to arrest same-sex couples. Fines on same-sex marriages were abolished by government decree on 24 September 2013, effective 11 November 2013.

Legal gender recognition rests on Article 37 of the 2015 Civil Code, passed by the National Assembly on 24 November 2015 by 282 votes to 84 and effective from January 2017. It allows people who have undergone sex reassignment to register under their preferred sex. A further implementing bill is still required, so the provision is not fully enforced. A law granting official transgender recognition that was promised for 2017 has not been implemented; a recognition draft law remained under consideration as of February 2026, seven years after the National Assembly was expected to complete a draft law by 2020.

Under the Law on Citizen Identification, effective 1 July 2024, transgender citizens may change their ID card when undergoing gender transition but must present confirmation documents, and the change's legal effect depends on the Gender Affirmation Law being passed first.

Sex reassignment surgery was previously illegal, which forced transgender people to travel to Thailand for the procedure.

Conversion therapy has been prohibited since 3 August 2022 under Dispatch No. 4132/BYT-PC from the Ministry of Health, which states that homosexuality, bisexuality and being transgender are not illnesses and that LGBTQ+ people may not be forced into "treatment". The dispatch also required enhanced public communication across medical facilities nationwide so that staff and patients better understand LGBTQ+ individuals, and advised that psychological support be provided by people with an understanding of gender identity. A study published by Lighthouse Vietnam in October 2024 documents the forms conversion efforts take in Vietnam and the experiences of LGBTIQ people subjected to them.

Healthcare access is uneven. Transgender women report routine discrimination at healthcare encounters, including being asked "Are you male or female? Why do you look so different to your ID card?", heightened scrutiny, and a risk of physical and sexual violence driven by economic pressure and stigma, with transgender women in northern provinces and from ethnic minorities particularly exposed. Providers themselves are often respectful; the obstacles are administrative, with implementing guidance for civil-status change stalled and policy gaps persisting.

Vietnamese law provides no protection from discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Amnesty International's 2025 assessment found that LGBTI people's rights lacked meaningful protection in both law and practice.

That gap sits within wider repression. Vague provisions of the Penal Code, articles 109, 116, 117 and 331, were used to arrest at least 43 people in 2025, and proposed press-law rules would compel disclosure of sources. Vietnam was re-elected to the UN Human Rights Council for a term running to 2028.

Public assembly has narrowed. In late 2025 Ho Chi Minh City abruptly cancelled its flagship Pride march and at least five other Pride events that year. Human Rights Watch's Asia director, Patricia Gossman, described the cancellations as worrying signs of a government clampdown on LGBTQ+ rights, set against Vietnam's reputation for tolerance in the region. The 2015 lifting of the ban on same-sex marriage left such unions without legal recognition.

Same-sex unions were removed from the list of forbidden acts but confer no rights. LGBTIQ organisations operate openly, though under government surveillance.
tangentialFactors:
No law prohibits non-consensual medical interventions on intersex people.

Media treatment has shifted over two decades. In 2002 publications such as Thế Giới Phụ Nữ and Tiếp thị & Gia đình described homosexuality as a disease and "deviant behavior"; in September 2010 Tuoi Tre Online became the first major state media outlet to state that homosexuality is normal. The 2013 sitcom My Best Gay Friends was published on YouTube because Vietnamese broadcasters were reluctant to air it.

Vietnam's first gay pride parade was held in Hanoi on 5 August 2012. By 2017 pride events were held in around 34 other cities and provinces, with more than 35 similar events annually in cities including Haiphong, Da Nang, Ho Chi Minh City and Cần Thơ. Hanoi Pride ran for a fifth consecutive year from 18 to 24 September 2017, drawing thousands against about a hundred at the first parade, and its sixth edition in November 2018 saw more than 1,000 participants cycle to campaign for transgender rights and same-sex marriage. Several events were aired on the state channels VTV4, VTV6 and VTV9.

A 2007 poll of 300 junior-high and high-school pupils at Ho Chi Minh City Pedagogical University found 80 per cent answered no to the question "Is homosexuality bad?". Pew data from 2023 shows support for same-sex marriage at 79 per cent among 18 to 34 year olds against 57 per cent among those aged 35 and above.

In 2006 the government enacted legislation protecting citizens infected with HIV and people living with AIDS from discrimination.
localsOnly:
A 2015 study found around 44 per cent of Vietnamese LGBT students aged 14 to 22 faced stigma, discrimination and violence because of their identities. A 2014 USAID report found 54 per cent of LGBT students said their school was not safe, with many dropping out; among those who experienced violence, one third thought about suicide and half of those attempted it. 85 per cent of transgender students said they dropped out because of assault and bullying. A 2015 UNESCO study found 19 per cent of students perceived bullying of LGBT students as "harmless", and 70 per cent of Hanoi parents said they would not allow their children to talk to gay students, some believing conversion therapy could "cure" LGBT children.

In January 2015 the Social, Economic and Environmental Institute proposed to the Ministry of Public Security that homosexual and transgender prisoners be housed separately from the general prison population to protect them from sexual harassment. The institute cited California statistics that 67 per cent of homosexual and transgender prisoners had suffered sexual harassment and a 2014 survey finding that most transgender prisoners wanted separate jails. It stated that under Vietnam's prison infrastructure at the time transgender prisoners could only be held in solitary confinement or mixed with the general population, meaning no housing wing matched to a prisoner's gender identity existed, and asked that prisoners be allowed to determine their own gender identity. No enacted outcome has been documented.

Health care is provided free to all Vietnamese citizens.
outOfScopeNotes:
The implementing bill required to give effect to Article 37 of the 2015 Civil Code remains unresolved. The National Assembly was expected to complete a draft law by 2020; as of February 2026 a recognition draft law was still under consideration. Whether a Gender Affirmation Law will pass, and what it will contain, is not sourced.

The 2015 proposal on separate prison housing for homosexual and transgender prisoners has no documented enacted outcome.

The Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada response to information request VNM201080.E is dated 30 June 2022 and predates the 2024 to 2026 developments described above; its finding on the absence of discrimination protection rests on Freedom House material dated 3 March 2021.
